title: Teaching Blogs: Who Needs Them?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles reflects on why he distrusts the endless fine-grained advice in popular teaching blogs. He does not say the advice is wrong, only that it misses the main point. He uses a marathon-training analogy drawn from his own competitive rowing, where obsessing over sleeves, socks and nutrition plans matters far less than simply doing intentional reps under pressure. Applied to teaching, getting better at questioning means asking many questions quickly in key parts of the lesson, finding what works, and never letting students off. He tells readers who want taxonomies of question types to read other bloggers, but recommends the simple, maintainable path of regular pressured practice because improvement shows immediately.
points: Detailed teaching advice can distract from the one thing that drives improvement: repeated, intentional practice.
Salles's rowing analogy shows that extra volume yields diminishing returns not worth doubling the workload.
To improve questioning, ask a great many questions quickly in key lesson phases and learn from student responses.
Students can answer far more questions than teachers assume, and repetition without letting anyone off improves retention.
quotes: But lately even the best bloggers have caused me some alarm. It isn’t that anything they are recommending is wrong. They write very well about aspects of teaching which make complete sense. It’s just that I think that they completely miss the main point.
The point of the analogy is this. The main thing you can do is reps. Intentional reps. Reps under pressure.
I could have obsessed over lots of long rows, many more miles, many more hours. And sure, I would have been faster. But not that much faster. Not enough to justify the doubling of workload.
You’ll work out which sort work, and which don’t, which to do orally, and which to put in a quiz. Most importantly, you’ll learn that students can answer many, many more questions than you think.
Keep it simple - that way it is easy to maintain. Do it regularly under pressure, and you will simply get better and better and better, because you will see student improvement straight away.
